Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

on the last line of your reply:

reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only

# Continual-ARC inference and interaction

Use for interactive Continual-ARC instances with a test grid, demonstration requests, and scored submissions.

## Protocol first

- On every turn, provide exactly one action JSON object on the last line: `{"action":"submit","grid":[...]}`, `{"action":"request_demos"}`, or `{"action":"finish"}`. Do not add prose or unrelated tool calls to puzzle turns.
- `finish` is only appropriate after the instance is over. Keep dimensions and cell values valid (rows/columns 1–30, values 0–9).
- Demonstration requests and wrong submissions have explicit costs. Use received evidence carefully; request another demo when it can resolve genuine ambiguity, rather than reflexively requesting or guessing.

## Infer from observed differences

1. Parse the entire input/output demo pair and identify exact cell changes, objects, colors, and spatial relationships. Distinguish unchanged elements from transformed ones.
2. Compare multiple demonstrations when available. Prefer the narrowest rule that explains all examples, including which components are preserved and how edge cases behave.
3. Do not assume a loaded ARC skill applies just because it is familiar; use its rule only when the observed demo supports it. In particular, do not infer stamping from a grid containing compact colored shapes and markers alone.
4. When the rule is underdetermined, request a demo specifically to distinguish plausible hypotheses. Avoid a low-information demo if a confident rule is already established.
5. Apply the inferred transformation to the test grid, preserving everything not implicated by the rule. Validate dimensions, row lengths, and that each changed cell follows the inferred rule before submitting.

A familiar task label or a visually plausible template is not evidence that a rule applies. Infer from actual input/output differences, compare multiple demonstrations, and avoid guessing transformations from visual intuition alone. Before submission validate every output row and only modify cells explained by the inferred rule.

## Validated partition-and-count rule (task-184e66d7)
Two demonstrations established a compact summary transformation: full-width horizontal dividers and/or full-height vertical dividers partition the grid into rectangular panels. Each panel contains a background color and isolated cells of one marker color. Output one cell per panel, preserving the panel layout/order; use output marker color 1 exactly for panels containing two marker cells, and use the input background color for panels with any other count. The 6-panel demo verified that zero- and one-marker panels map to background while two-marker panels map to 1; the other demo verified one- versus two-marker panels. On the 11x14 test (background 6, marker 5, dividers 3), the 3x3 output `[[1,6,1],[6,1,6],[1,1,1]]` was accepted. This is a counting/partitioning rule, not template stamping. Re-identify complete separator lines and count marker cells per compartment; don't count separator cells or infer from marker positions alone.

## Paired bars project a scattered marker pattern (task-345ec273)
Two equal-length, same-color bars embedded in the background can define the ends of rows to complete. In the demonstrations, one bar was vertical at a grid edge in an upper/lower region and the other bar occupied corresponding rows/columns in another region; isolated marker-color cells between/near the bars determined which row offsets to draw. For each marker's offset within one bar's span, extend a straight marker-color line across the gap toward the opposing bar, changing the marker endpoint to color 4. Copy the same offset pattern to the corresponding span of the other bar and draw a line across its gap as well. Preserve both bars, all background outside these line segments, and other cells. In task-345ec273, the 4-cell 5-bars were at left rows 0–3 and right rows 6–9; marker 2 positions relative to the right bar were `[col 1, col 2, col 1, col 1]`. The output extended 2 across the gap on those four rows in both spans, and changed the four original marker cells to 4. The distinct demo had vertical 8-bars of length 5; marker-row offsets `{0,2,3,4}` were extended from the left bar to each marker (marker becomes 4) and repeated across the upper bar span. The input/output confirms the selected row/offset pattern is projected to the corresponding second bar, not filled indiscriminately across every row. Maintain the existing grid dimensions and don't recolor the bars or unrelated cells.

## Binary palette inversion into zero with background recoloring (task-33198301)
Across five demos with varying palette pairs, each grid contained a dominant background color `B` and sparse contrasting cells of color `M`; outputs consistently mapped every `B` cell to 0 and every `M` cell to the original background `B`. Examples: 5/7 became 7/0, 9/5 became 0/9, 2/5 became 0/2, 1/5 became 0/1, and 5/6 became 0/5. Apply this as a global two-color substitution, preserving dimensions; do not simply map the sparse marker to zero or assume a fixed output color. The 22x30 test with background 9 and sparse 5 was accepted with `9→0` and `5→9`.

This session exposed a recurring validation issue for region-filling puzzles. Demos showed that the fill target can be fully contained by a boundary that touches the canvas border. A flood fill which seeds all background cells along the grid edge then treats the target as exterior, even though the demos establish it as an enclosed cavity.

## Reliable analysis

1. Compare demo input/output cell-by-cell and record the exact changed coordinates. Identify the connected outline and each altered component, including whether a component touches a grid edge.
2. Verify the rule against all available examples before transferring it to a differently shaped test. Do not infer that every background component adjacent to an edge should be filled.
3. For each candidate target, identify a closed perimeter in the actual geometry. The canvas frame may complete part of that perimeter only if the demos demonstrate that edge-touching cavities are filled.
4. A border-seeded flood fill is useful for cavities fully enclosed by grid cells, but is not sufficient when the grid edge itself participates in a demonstrated enclosure. Either model the perimeter-plus-frame explicitly or classify candidate regions by their demonstrated outline relationship.
5. Preserve the outline and all unrelated cells. Validate exact row count, width, and changed coordinates before submission.

## Pitfall from this interaction

The test contained an irregular outline touching the lower and left edges and a vertical segment near the right side. A guessed set of edge-adjacent rectangles was submitted without a full demo-validated perimeter analysis and was incorrect. The reliable lesson is not a specific fill mask: it is to use the demos to determine exactly which boundary geometry qualifies and avoid hand-selecting rectangles. The full demos and test from this session remain in the conversation transcript; no unverified test output is asserted here.
